title: The ENT Examination and Hearing Tests
summary: Learn the bedside and instrument-based tests used to examine the ears, balance, nose and larynx.

lessons.title: Otoscopy and Pneumatic Otoscopy

levels.kid:
Your ear has a tiny tunnel that leads to a thin, round skin called the **eardrum**. It works like the skin on a real drum. When sound hits it, it wiggles, and that helps you hear.

Doctors look down the tunnel with a small flashlight called an **otoscope**. It has a cone tip that fits gently in your ear. To see better, the doctor pulls your ear softly to straighten the tunnel.

A healthy eardrum looks pearly gray, a bit like a shiny shell. A sick one can look red and puffy.

Sometimes the doctor puffs a little air into your ear. A healthy eardrum wiggles. If there is goo behind it, it barely moves, like a drum filled with water.
levels.hs:
An **otoscope** is a handheld light with a magnifying lens and a cone-shaped tip called a **speculum**. It lets a clinician look down the **external ear canal** at the **tympanic membrane** (eardrum), the thin layer that separates the outer ear from the air-filled **middle ear**.

How it is done:
- Pick the largest speculum that fits comfortably.
- Straighten the curved canal. In adults, pull the outer ear **up and back**. In young children, pull it **down and back**.
- Brace the hand holding the otoscope against the patient's head, so a sudden movement does not push the tip into the canal.

A normal eardrum is **pearly gray and translucent**. You can see the handle of the **malleus** (the first tiny ear bone) and a bright triangle of reflected light, the **cone of light**.

**Pneumatic otoscopy** adds a rubber bulb that puffs air into a sealed canal. A healthy eardrum moves back and forth. If fluid fills the middle ear, the drum barely moves.

Real example: a 2-year-old has a fever and pulls at one ear. The eardrum is red, **bulging**, and does not move with air. That pattern fits **acute otitis media**, a middle-ear infection.
levels.college:
Otoscopy examines the external auditory canal (EAC) and tympanic membrane (TM). The lateral third of the EAC is cartilaginous and hair-bearing, where cerumen is made. The medial two-thirds is bony and lined with thin, very sensitive skin, so pressing on it hurts. Pulling the pinna **posterosuperiorly** in adults (posteroinferiorly in infants) straightens the canal.

**Normal TM landmarks:**
- **Pars tensa**: the large, taut lower portion
- **Pars flaccida**: a small, lax area above the lateral process of the malleus
- **Umbo**: the tip of the malleus handle, at the center of the drum
- **Cone of light**: points **anteroinferiorly**, so it sits at about 5 o'clock in the right ear and 7 o'clock in the left
- Sometimes the long process of the **incus** shows through the posterosuperior quadrant

**Pneumatic otoscopy** needs an airtight seal with a speculum that fits snugly. Squeezing the bulb raises canal pressure and the TM moves inward; releasing it moves the TM outward. Mobility can be normal, reduced or absent, or excessive (in a thin, scarred segment).

**Key findings:**
- **Acute otitis media (AOM)**: a bulging, opaque, often red TM with poor mobility. Bulging is the most specific sign. Redness alone is weak evidence, because crying also reddens the drum.
- **Otitis media with effusion (OME)**: a retracted or neutral, dull TM. Air-fluid levels or bubbles may be visible. Mobility is reduced, and there are no acute signs.
- **Perforation**: a hole in the drum, and the drum does not move.
- **Retraction pocket**: the drum is sucked inward, often in the pars flaccida.
- **Otitis externa**: a swollen, tender canal. Pulling on the pinna or pressing the **tragus** hurts.
- **Cholesteatoma**: white keratin debris, classically in the attic (above the pars flaccida).

In children, pneumatic otoscopy is the recommended primary method for diagnosing OME.
levels.phd:
The TM is a three-layer structure. It has an outer epidermis continuous with the canal skin, a middle **lamina propria** (fibrous layer), and an inner mucosa. In the pars tensa, the lamina propria contains radial and circular collagen fibers that give the drum its stiffness. The pars flaccida lacks this organized fibrous layer. That is why it gives way under chronic negative pressure and is the classic site of **attic retraction** and **acquired cholesteatoma**.

Pneumatic otoscopy is a crude, qualitative test of how easily the middle ear moves under pressure. Fluid in the middle ear raises the stiffness and mass of the system, which dampens TM movement. A hypermobile drum reflects thinned segments with less collagen (**dimeric membrane** or atrophic scar) or, rarely, a disarticulated ossicular chain.

Accuracy data matter. In the Takata et al. meta-analysis (Pediatrics 2003), pneumatic otoscopy for middle-ear effusion had a pooled sensitivity of about 94% and specificity of about 80%, better than plain otoscopy. Performance depends heavily on the examiner. Validation studies use **myringotomy** findings as the reference standard.

AOM diagnosis has been tightened to limit overdiagnosis and antibiotic overuse. The **AAP 2013** guideline requires one of the following:
- moderate to severe bulging of the TM
- new **otorrhea** (ear discharge) not due to otitis externa
- mild bulging plus recent ear pain or intense TM redness

There must also be middle-ear effusion. Shaikh and Hoberman's work identified bulging as the single most discriminating feature between AOM and OME.

Perforations are described by quadrant and by margin. **Central** perforations leave a rim of TM around the hole. **Marginal** perforations reach the annulus. Marginal and attic defects carry a higher risk of cholesteatoma, because squamous epithelium can migrate inward through them.

There is ongoing debate about how good otoscopy really is outside specialist settings. Studies of primary-care clinicians and trainees show only moderate agreement between examiners, partly due to cerumen, poor seals and uncooperative children. This argues for structured training and for objective tests as a supplement.
levels.expert:
In practice, most failed otoscopic exams come from technique, not from missing knowledge. Common pitfalls:
- **Wrong speculum size**: too small and no seal forms, so a falsely immobile drum suggests effusion that is not there.
- **Battery-dimmed halogen light**: this distorts color and makes a normal drum look dull or yellow.
- **Crying child**: crying causes redness through hyperemia and makes the pressure seal harder to hold.
- **Cerumen**: this blocks a meaningful share of pediatric exams. It can be removed by curette, irrigation or suction. Irrigation is avoided when a perforation or grommet may be present, and caution is needed when the patient has diabetes, given concern for necrotizing otitis externa.

**Red flags at the bedside:**
- **Granulation tissue on the canal floor** in an older patient with diabetes or immunocompromise and severe ear pain suggests **necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa**, a skull-base osteomyelitis usually caused by *Pseudomonas*. It needs imaging and specialist care.
- **Attic crust or a persistent discharging "perforation"** may hide a cholesteatoma. Remove the crust or get microscopy before calling it benign.
- **A blue or red mass behind an intact drum** has a differential that includes a **glomus tympanicum** paraganglioma (often pulsatile, and it may blanch with positive pressure, called **Brown's sign**), a high or dehiscent jugular bulb, or an aberrant carotid artery. Biopsying a vascular retrotympanic mass before imaging is a classic, dangerous error.
- **Vesicles in the concha or canal** with facial weakness point to **Ramsay Hunt syndrome**.
- **Hemotympanum** or canal laceration after head trauma suggests a temporal bone fracture, which matters to neurosurgical teams.

ENT clinics favor the **binocular operating microscope** and **endoscopes** (0° and 30°) over the handheld otoscope. These give depth perception and two free hands for suction.

**Recent advances:**
- **Smartphone otoscopes** support telemedicine.
- **Deep-learning classifiers** have been trained on TM images, with reported accuracy approaching or exceeding non-specialists in research datasets. Generalization across devices and populations is still unproven.
- **Optical coherence tomography** otoscopes and **short-wave infrared** imaging can visualize middle-ear fluid and biofilm more objectively.

An open question is whether these tools will reduce AOM overdiagnosis in real primary care, or simply shift where the uncertainty lies.

keyPoints: An otoscope views the ear canal and tympanic membrane through a speculum
Pull the pinna up and back in adults, down and back in infants
A normal eardrum is pearly gray with the malleus and an anteroinferior cone of light
Pneumatic otoscopy tests eardrum mobility; fluid reduces movement
Bulging is the most specific sign of acute otitis media
Pars flaccida retraction and attic debris raise concern for cholesteatoma

test.q: To straighten the ear canal of an adult during otoscopy, the clinician pulls the pinna:
test.explain: Pulling up and back straightens the adult canal. Down and back is the technique used for young children.

test.q: A healthy tympanic membrane usually appears:
test.explain: A normal drum is pearly gray and translucent. Redness, opacity or bubbles suggest disease.

test.q: In which direction does the cone of light normally point?
test.explain: The light reflex points anteroinferiorly, at about 5 o'clock in the right ear and 7 o'clock in the left.

test.q: What does pneumatic otoscopy add to a standard exam?
choices: A measure of hearing at each pitch
test.explain: Puffing air into a sealed canal shows whether the drum moves. Fluid behind it dampens that movement.

test.q: Which finding is the most specific for acute otitis media?
test.explain: Bulging is the most discriminating sign. Redness alone is weak evidence because crying can redden the drum.

test.q: A retracted, dull eardrum with bubbles and poor mobility but no acute signs suggests:
test.explain: OME shows middle-ear fluid without signs of acute infection such as bulging.

test.q: Pain when the tragus is pressed and a swollen canal point to:
test.explain: Otitis externa inflames the canal skin, so moving the tragus or pinna hurts.

test.q: White keratin debris above the pars flaccida (the attic) is classic for:
test.explain: Attic keratin debris is the textbook appearance of acquired cholesteatoma.

test.q: Why does the medial ear canal hurt when the speculum presses on it?
choices: It is bone lined with thin, sensitive skin
It is covered by middle-ear mucosa
It is cartilage with thick, hairy skin
It contains the glands that make wax
test.explain: The medial two-thirds is bony and covered by thin, sensitive skin. The lateral third is the cartilaginous, hair-bearing part.

test.q: The cone-shaped tip of an otoscope that enters the ear canal is called the ___.
test.explain: Choosing the right speculum size matters for comfort and for forming an air seal.

test.q: What is the medical name for the eardrum?
test.explain: The tympanic membrane separates the external canal from the middle ear.

test.q: The tip of the malleus handle at the center of the eardrum is called the ___.
test.explain: The umbo is a key landmark, and the cone of light spreads out from it.

kidTest.q: What tool does a doctor use to look in your ear?
kidTest.explain: An otoscope is a small light with a cone tip for looking into ears.

kidTest.q: What color is a healthy eardrum?
kidTest.explain: A healthy eardrum is pearly gray, like a shiny shell.

kidTest.q: Why does the doctor gently pull your ear?
kidTest.explain: Pulling straightens the ear tunnel so the doctor can see the eardrum.

kidTest.q: If there is goo behind the eardrum, a puff of air makes it:
kidTest.explain: Fluid behind the drum stops it from wiggling, like a drum filled with water.

kidTest.q: The thin skin at the end of your ear tunnel is your ear d _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The eardrum wiggles when sound hits it.

advancedTest.q: A child has a falsely immobile drum on pneumatic otoscopy, but tympanometry later shows a normal middle ear. The most likely technical cause was:
choices: Pulling the pinna down and back
A speculum too small to form a seal
Excess light from a new halogen bulb
A speculum too large for the canal
advancedTest.explain: Without an airtight seal, air leaks out and the drum seems not to move, which mimics an effusion.

advancedTest.q: Why is the pars flaccida the usual site of attic retraction and cholesteatoma?
choices: It has a thicker epidermis prone to shedding keratin
It lacks the organized collagen of the lamina propria
It is supplied by a separate arterial branch
It sits directly over the round window niche
advancedTest.explain: Without radial and circular collagen fibers, the pars flaccida gives way under chronic negative middle-ear pressure.

advancedTest.q: A pulsatile red mass behind an intact drum blanches with positive pneumatic pressure. What is the best next step?
choices: A course of topical antibiotic drops
advancedTest.explain: Brown's sign suggests a vascular lesion such as a glomus tympanicum. Biopsy before imaging risks severe bleeding.

advancedTest.q: A crying infant has an intensely red eardrum with normal mobility and no bulging. Under AAP 2013 criteria, this most supports:
choices: No firm diagnosis of acute otitis media
advancedTest.explain: AOM requires a middle-ear effusion plus bulging or new otorrhea. Normal mobility argues against effusion, and crying can cause redness.

lessons.title: Tuning Fork Tests: Weber and Rinne

levels.kid:
A tuning fork is a metal tool shaped like a big letter Y. When you tap it, it hums a clear note.

Sound can reach your inner ear in two ways. It can travel through the **air** into your ear hole. It can also travel through your **bones**, like when you hear your own teeth crunching a carrot.

Doctors use the humming fork for two games. In the **Weber** test, they put the fork on top of your head and ask, "Is it louder on one side?" In the **Rinne** test, they hold it on the bone behind your ear, then next to your ear, and ask which is louder.

Your answers help the doctor guess whether sound is getting blocked, like by earwax, or whether the hearing part deep inside is weaker.
levels.hs:
Hearing loss comes in two main types:
- **Conductive hearing loss**: sound can't get through the outer or middle ear. Causes include earwax, fluid behind the eardrum, or a hole in the eardrum.
- **Sensorineural hearing loss**: the problem is in the **cochlea** (the inner ear's hearing organ) or the hearing nerve.

Tuning fork tests can tell these apart at the bedside in under a minute. Doctors usually use a **512 Hz** fork, struck gently on a knee or elbow.

The **Weber test**: the fork is placed on the middle of the forehead or top of the head. Vibrations travel through the skull to both inner ears. Normally the sound is heard in the middle. In conductive loss, it sounds **louder in the bad ear**. In sensorineural loss, it sounds **louder in the good ear**.

The **Rinne test**: the fork is placed on the **mastoid bone** behind the ear (bone conduction), then held beside the ear canal (air conduction). Normally air conduction is louder, because the eardrum and middle-ear bones amplify sound. This is called a **positive Rinne**. If bone sounds louder, that's a **negative Rinne**, which suggests conductive loss.

Example: a child with fluid in the right middle ear after a cold has a Weber that goes to the right and a negative Rinne on the right. That pattern means conductive loss on the right.
levels.college:
Tuning fork tests compare **air conduction (AC)**, which depends on the external canal, tympanic membrane and ossicles, with **bone conduction (BC)**, which largely bypasses them and stimulates the cochlea directly through skull vibration.

**Technique.** A 512 Hz fork is the standard: 256 Hz produces vibrations felt as touch, and higher frequencies decay too quickly. Strike it on a firm but soft surface such as the knee, elbow or a rubber pad, not a hard surface, which creates overtones.

**Weber.** Place the base on the vertex, forehead or upper incisors. Ask where the sound is heard.
- Midline: normal, or symmetric loss.
- Lateralizes to the **affected** ear: ipsilateral conductive loss.
- Lateralizes to the **better** ear: contralateral sensorineural loss.
Conductive lateralization is explained by the **occlusion effect** (bone-conducted energy escaping less from a blocked ear) and loss of masking ambient noise in that ear.

**Rinne.** Place the fork on the mastoid until the sound fades, then move the tines near the canal (or compare loudness directly).
- **Positive (AC > BC)**: normal, or sensorineural loss (both reduced, ratio preserved).
- **Negative (BC > AC)**: conductive loss, typically with an air-bone gap of roughly 20 dB or more at 512 Hz.

**Interpreting together.**
- Weber to the left + left Rinne negative = left conductive loss.
- Weber to the left + both Rinne positive = right sensorineural loss.

**False negative Rinne.** In a severe unilateral sensorineural loss, the bone-conducted sound crosses the skull and is heard by the **opposite cochlea**, so the patient reports BC > AC on the dead side. Clues: Weber goes to the good ear, and masking the good ear with a noise source (a **Bárány box**) abolishes the response.
levels.phd:
The physics of bone conduction explains both tests. Skull vibration excites the cochlea through several routes: **compressional** (direct deformation of the otic capsule), **inertial** (lag of the ossicular chain relative to the skull, so the stapes moves in the oval window), and **osseotympanic** (sound radiated into the external canal by vibrating canal walls). Inner-ear fluid inertia and the third-window properties of the cochlear aqueduct contribute too.

In **conductive loss**, the osseotympanic route is enhanced when the canal is occluded (the **occlusion effect**, maximal below about 1 kHz, which also partly underlies the **Bing test**), and the ear loses ambient noise masking. Ossicular fixation also alters the inertial component: the classic **Carhart notch**, an apparent BC drop near 2 kHz in otosclerosis, reflects loss of ossicular inertial bone conduction rather than cochlear damage, and often resolves after stapedotomy.

**Interaural attenuation** for bone conduction is close to 0 dB, versus roughly 40 dB or more for air conduction with supra-aural earphones. Any bone-conducted stimulus is therefore effectively delivered to both cochleae, which is why the Weber works at all and why a unilateral dead ear yields a false negative Rinne. Audiometric masking principles derive from the same fact.

**Sensitivity.** The Weber detects fairly small asymmetries but cannot quantify them. The Rinne at 512 Hz becomes reliably negative only once the air-bone gap reaches around 20 to 30 dB; smaller gaps produce false positives. Studies comparing tuning forks with audiometry report high specificity but only moderate sensitivity for mild conductive loss, with results depending on striking force, fork frequency and examiner technique. Using 256 Hz increases sensitivity for small gaps but adds vibrotactile confounding.

**Variants.** The **Schwabach** test compares the patient's BC duration with the examiner's (shortened in sensorineural loss). The **absolute bone conduction** test does the same with the external canal occluded. The **Bing** test asks whether occluding the canal makes BC louder: positive in normal and sensorineural ears, absent in conductive loss. These are mainly historical, superseded by pure-tone audiometry.
levels.expert:
In practice the tuning fork remains a triage tool whose highest-stakes use is **sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL)**. A patient reporting abrupt unilateral hearing loss may simply have impacted wax or a middle-ear effusion, or may have a cochlear injury in which early treatment (typically corticosteroids, per AAO-HNS guidance) is time-sensitive. A Weber lateralizing to the **unaffected** ear with a positive Rinne on the affected side points to SSNHL and warrants same-day audiometry and ENT input. Patients with unexplained asymmetric sensorineural loss also need evaluation for retrocochlear pathology such as **vestibular schwannoma**, usually with MRI.

Pitfalls worth knowing:
- **Supranormal bone conduction.** **Superior semicircular canal dehiscence** acts as a third mobile window, shunting air-conducted energy away from the cochlea while enhancing bone conduction. It can produce a negative Rinne and an air-bone gap mimicking otosclerosis, yet stapedial reflexes are preserved. Some patients hear a tuning fork placed on the ankle (medial malleolus). Mistaking this for otosclerosis risks unnecessary stapes surgery.
- **Mixed loss.** A Weber can sit midline or mislead when conductive and sensorineural components coexist; the forks cannot separate them.
- **Unreliable reporters.** Young children, patients with cognitive impairment, and those with nonorganic hearing loss give inconsistent answers. A Weber claimed to the "deaf" side combined with a denied BC response raises suspicion of functional loss.
- **Technique drift.** Striking too hard creates overtones and a louder, longer stimulus, inflating apparent AC > BC.

Intraoperatively, otologists sometimes use a fork after stapes surgery or tympanoplasty as a quick check that conduction has improved, and before surgery for otosclerosis the Rinne helps confirm that the gap is large enough for surgery to offer meaningful benefit.

Open questions are mostly about standardization: electronic vibrators with calibrated output, smartphone-based bone-conduction screening, and whether structured fork testing improves primary-care triage of SSNHL. None replaces formal audiometry, which is covered in the next lesson.

keyPoints: Air conduction uses the outer and middle ear; bone conduction stimulates the cochlea directly
Use a 512 Hz fork struck on a knee or elbow
Weber lateralizes to the conductive-loss ear and away from the sensorineural-loss ear
Rinne positive (air louder than bone) is normal or sensorineural; negative suggests conductive loss
A dead ear can give a false negative Rinne because the other cochlea hears the bone vibration
Sudden unilateral sensorineural loss is urgent; forks help separate it from wax or fluid

test.q: Which tuning fork frequency is standard for Weber and Rinne testing?
test.explain: 512 Hz balances a long enough tone with little vibrotactile sensation. 256 Hz is more easily felt as touch.

test.q: In the Weber test, where is the fork placed?
choices: Just beside the external ear canal
On the zygomatic bone of the cheek
On the mastoid bone behind the ear
On the forehead at the midline
test.explain: Weber uses a midline point such as the forehead or vertex so vibration reaches both cochleae equally.

test.q: A patient with right-sided conductive loss will most likely hear the Weber:
test.explain: In conductive loss, Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, partly because of the occlusion effect.

test.q: A patient with left sensorineural loss will most likely hear the Weber:
test.explain: In sensorineural loss the damaged cochlea responds less, so sound is heard in the better (right) ear.

test.q: A normal Rinne result is described as:
test.explain: Normally air conduction is louder because the eardrum and ossicles amplify sound; this is a positive Rinne.

test.q: A negative Rinne in one ear most suggests:
test.explain: Bone conduction louder than air conduction means sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear.

test.q: Weber lateralizes left and both Rinne tests are positive. The likely diagnosis is:
test.explain: Positive Rinnes rule against conductive loss, and Weber goes away from the sensorineural ear, so the right ear is affected.

test.q: Why can a severely deaf ear give a false negative Rinne?
choices: Its eardrum vibrates much more strongly
Its middle ear amplifies the bone sound
The fork's tone decays faster on that side
The other cochlea hears the vibration
test.explain: Bone-conducted sound crosses the skull with almost no attenuation, so the good cochlea responds and the patient reports bone louder.

test.q: Why should the fork be struck on a knee or elbow rather than a table?
choices: It keeps the fork from cooling
Soft surfaces make it last longer
test.explain: Striking a hard surface produces overtones and an uneven stimulus, which distorts the test.

test.q: In the Rinne test, bone conduction is checked by placing the fork on the ___ bone behind the ear.
test.explain: The mastoid process transmits vibration through the skull to the cochlea.

test.q: What type of hearing loss is caused by earwax, middle-ear fluid or a perforated eardrum?
test.explain: These problems block sound in the outer or middle ear, which is conductive loss.

test.q: What device can be used to mask the better ear when testing a suspected dead ear?
test.explain: A Bárány noise box masks the good ear so it cannot respond to crossed-over bone conduction.

kidTest.q: What does a tuning fork do when you tap it?
choices: It blows a puff of air
kidTest.explain: A tapped tuning fork vibrates and hums.

kidTest.q: In the Weber test, where does the doctor put the fork?
kidTest.explain: The fork goes on the middle of the head so both ears can hear it.

kidTest.q: Besides air, what else can carry sound to your inner ear?
kidTest.explain: Sound can travel through bones, like when you hear yourself crunch a carrot.

kidTest.q: What could block sound from getting into the ear?
kidTest.explain: Earwax can block the ear canal so sound gets through less well.

kidTest.q: A metal tool shaped like a Y hums when the doctor taps it. It is called a tuning f _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: It's called a tuning fork because it looks a bit like a fork.

advancedTest.q: Why does a single midline Weber stimulus reach both cochleae almost equally?
choices: Bone conduction interaural attenuation is close to 0 dB
The cochlear aqueduct links the two inner ears together
The ossicles transmit vibration to the opposite middle ear
Air conduction has very low interaural attenuation through the canals
advancedTest.explain: Skull vibration crosses to both sides with almost no loss, which is also why a dead ear can give a false negative Rinne.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a negative Rinne and an air-bone gap but preserved stapedial reflexes and hears a fork on the ankle. The most likely cause is:
advancedTest.explain: A third window enhances bone conduction and mimics conductive loss, but reflexes stay intact, unlike in otosclerosis.

advancedTest.q: The Carhart notch near 2 kHz in otosclerosis is best explained by:
choices: Loss of the ossicular inertial component of bone conduction
Damage to the cochlear nerve from the disease
An enhanced occlusion effect at high frequencies
Hair cell loss in the basal turn of the cochlea
advancedTest.explain: It reflects altered ossicular inertia, not cochlear damage, which is why it often improves after stapedotomy.

advancedTest.q: Why can a patient with a mild conductive loss still have a positive Rinne at 512 Hz?
choices: Positive Rinne results are specific to sensorineural loss
Air-bone gaps under about 20 to 30 dB are missed
Mild conductive loss raises air conduction above normal
A 512 Hz fork mainly stimulates the opposite cochlea
advancedTest.explain: The Rinne has moderate sensitivity: it becomes reliably negative only once the air-bone gap reaches about 20 to 30 dB, so small gaps give false positives.

lessons.title: Pure-Tone Audiometry and Tympanometry

levels.kid:
Your ears are like tiny microphones that send sound messages to your brain. Doctors have special games to check how well they work.

In one game, you sit in a quiet booth wearing headphones. You hear little beeps, some high like a bird and some low like a drum. Every time you hear a beep, even a super quiet one, you press a button. The quietest beep you can hear is written on a chart called an **audiogram**.

In another test, the doctor puts a soft plug in your ear. It gently pushes a little air in and out. This checks whether your eardrum wiggles the way it should. If there is gooey fluid behind it, like after a cold, the eardrum barely moves. It takes only a few seconds and does not hurt.
levels.hs:
**Pure-tone audiometry** measures the softest sound a person can hear at different pitches. Pitch is measured in **hertz (Hz)**, and the test usually covers 250 to 8000 Hz. Loudness is measured in **decibels hearing level (dB HL)**, where 0 dB HL is the average threshold of young adults with healthy ears. The softest level you can detect about half the time is your **threshold**.

The results are plotted on an **audiogram**. Pitch runs left to right and loudness runs top to bottom, so worse hearing sits lower on the chart. Two kinds of testing are done:
- **Air conduction**: sound through headphones travels through the whole ear.
- **Bone conduction**: a vibrator behind the ear sends sound through the skull straight to the inner ear, skipping the outer and middle ear.

If air is worse than bone (an **air-bone gap**), the problem is in the outer or middle ear. This is **conductive hearing loss**. If both are equally poor, the problem is in the inner ear or nerve. This is **sensorineural hearing loss**.

**Tympanometry** checks how easily the eardrum moves as air pressure in the ear canal changes. A flat result in a child after a cold usually means fluid behind the eardrum (otitis media with effusion), a common cause of mild temporary hearing loss.
levels.college:
**Pure-tone audiometry** is the behavioral gold standard for hearing thresholds. Tones are presented at octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz, sometimes with half-octaves at 3000 and 6000 Hz. The **modified Hughson-Westlake** method is used: descend 10 dB after each response and ascend 5 dB after each miss. Threshold is the lowest level heard on at least 2 of 3 ascending trials.

On the standard audiogram, right-ear air conduction is a red O and left-ear air conduction is a blue X. Unmasked bone conduction is < for the right and > for the left; masked bone uses brackets.

Common severity bands (one widely used scheme) based on the **pure-tone average (PTA)** of 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz:
- Normal: up to 25 dB HL
- Mild: 26-40
- Moderate: 41-55 (moderately severe 56-70)
- Severe: 71-90
- Profound: over 90

An **air-bone gap** of more than 10 dB points to conductive loss. **Masking** (narrowband noise in the non-test ear) prevents **cross-hearing**. Sound crosses the skull at about 40 dB or more with supra-aural headphones, but bone conduction crosses with almost no loss.

**Tympanometry** varies canal pressure from about +200 to -400 daPa while a probe tone (226 Hz in adults) measures admittance. The **Jerger types** are:
- **Type A**: normal peak near 0 daPa
- **As**: shallow peak (stiff system, e.g. otosclerosis)
- **Ad**: very tall peak (ossicular discontinuity or a floppy drum)
- **Type B**: flat. With normal canal volume it means effusion. With a large volume it means a perforation or patent tube. With a small volume it means wax or the probe pressed against the canal wall.
- **Type C**: negative peak pressure (Eustachian tube dysfunction)

**Acoustic reflexes** (stapedius contraction to loud sound) add information about the facial nerve and auditory brainstem pathway.
levels.phd:
Behavioral thresholds reflect the whole auditory system integrated over time. This is why audiometry is paired with physiologic measures. The dB HL scale is referenced to standardized threshold values (ISO 389). It converts the curved minimal audible field, where human hearing is most sensitive around 2-4 kHz, into a flat 0 line. This makes deviations from normal easy to see.

Audiometric shapes carry diagnostic meaning:
- **Noise-induced hearing loss** produces a notch at 3-6 kHz (classically 4 kHz) with recovery at 8 kHz. This pattern likely reflects ear-canal resonance and the mechanical vulnerability of the basal-middle cochlea.
- **Presbycusis** gives a sloping high-frequency loss.
- **Ménière disease** typically starts with a fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss.
- **Otosclerosis** shows the **Carhart notch**: an apparent bone-conduction dip of roughly 10-15 dB centered near 2 kHz. It is a mechanical artifact, because stapes fixation removes the middle ear's contribution to bone conduction, and it often improves after stapes surgery.

The **masking dilemma** arises with large bilateral conductive losses: masking noise loud enough to work may itself cross over to the test ear. Interaural attenuation is about 40 dB for supra-aural earphones, about 55-60 dB or more for insert earphones, and roughly 0-10 dB for bone.

Tympanometry measures **acoustic admittance** (Y), which combines susceptance (B) and conductance (G). At 226 Hz, the middle ear behaves as a stiffness-dominated system. Peak compensated static admittance in adults is roughly 0.3-1.7 mmho, and equivalent canal volume about 0.6-2.0 mL. In infants under about 6 months, the ear canal walls are compliant and the system is mass-influenced. A 226 Hz probe can give falsely normal peaks despite effusion, so a **1000 Hz probe tone** is recommended.

**Acoustic reflex** patterns help localize lesions. The reflex arc runs from the cochlea through CN VIII to the cochlear nucleus, then to the superior olivary complex on both sides, then the facial motor nucleus, then the stapedius. Absent reflexes with only mild hearing loss, or **reflex decay**, raise concern for retrocochlear pathology. An example is vestibular schwannoma.
levels.expert:
Clinical decision points that depend on these tests:

**Sudden sensorineural hearing loss** is defined (AAO-HNS guideline) as at least 30 dB loss over 3 consecutive frequencies within 72 hours. It is an otologic urgency. Audiometry, not tuning forks alone, confirms the diagnosis and provides the baseline. Prompt steroid therapy is time-sensitive, and MRI with gadolinium is used to exclude vestibular schwannoma.

**Asymmetric sensorineural loss** prompts MRI of the internal auditory canals. Asymmetry criteria vary by protocol: one common cutoff is at least 15 dB at 2 or more frequencies, and others use the 3000 Hz-only rule. Speech audiometry adds value here. A **word recognition score** disproportionately poor for the pure-tone level, or **rollover** at high presentation levels, suggests retrocochlear disease.

Pitfalls to watch for:
- **Collapsing ear canals** under supra-aural headphones can create a spurious high-frequency conductive gap, especially in elderly patients. Insert earphones prevent this.
- **Third-window lesions** such as superior canal dehiscence produce a low-frequency air-bone gap with supranormal bone thresholds, sometimes negative dB HL. Tympanometry is normal and acoustic reflexes are present. This combination mimics otosclerosis, but operating on the stapes will not help, and reflexes are typically absent in otosclerosis.
- **Functional (nonorganic) hearing loss** shows up as poor test-retest reliability, PTA-SRT disagreement beyond about 10 dB, and absent shadow curves despite unmasked unilateral 'deafness.' Otoacoustic emissions and ABR settle the question.
- A Type B tympanogram with high volume in a child with tubes means the tubes are open, which is good.

**Frontiers:**
- **Extended high-frequency audiometry** (above 8 to 16 kHz) detects early ototoxicity from cisplatin and aminoglycosides earlier than conventional testing. ASHA-style monitoring protocols use it.
- **Wideband acoustic immittance** (about 226-8000 Hz absorbance) improves detection of infant effusion and otosclerosis.
- **Boothless and smartphone audiometry** extends screening to underserved settings.
- **Hidden hearing loss** is a cochlear synaptopathy model from Kujawa and Liberman's 2009 mouse noise studies. It suggests normal audiograms can hide loss of synapses between inner hair cells and nerve fibers, but how common this is in humans remains debated.

keyPoints: Pure-tone audiometry finds hearing thresholds from 250-8000 Hz in dB HL
An air-bone gap over 10 dB means conductive loss; equal loss means sensorineural
Masking prevents cross-hearing to the non-test ear
Tympanometry measures eardrum admittance as canal pressure changes
Jerger types: A normal, B flat (effusion, perforation, wax), C negative pressure
Patterns: 4 kHz noise notch, Carhart notch in otosclerosis, low-tone Ménière loss

test.q: On an audiogram, what does the vertical axis show?
test.explain: Loudness (dB HL) runs top to bottom, with worse hearing plotted lower. Frequency runs along the horizontal axis.

test.q: Bone conduction is normal but air conduction is 30 dB worse. What type of loss is this?
test.explain: An air-bone gap means the inner ear works but sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear.

test.q: A child's tympanogram is flat with a normal canal volume. What is the most likely cause?
test.explain: A Type B tracing with normal volume suggests fluid behind the eardrum. A perforation would give a large volume.

test.q: A Type C tympanogram most suggests:
test.explain: Type C has a peak at negative pressure, meaning the Eustachian tube is not ventilating the middle ear well.

test.q: Why is masking noise used during audiometry?
choices: To keep the other ear out of the test
To measure how well the eardrum moves
To cover up noise from outside the booth
To make the test tones easier to detect
test.explain: Masking prevents cross-hearing, where sound crosses the skull to the better ear.

test.q: Which frequencies make up the standard pure-tone average?
test.explain: The classic PTA averages thresholds at 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz, the key speech frequencies.

test.q: A notch at about 4000 Hz with recovery at 8000 Hz is classic for:
test.explain: Noise damage produces a 3-6 kHz notch. Presbycusis slopes downward without recovery.

test.q: A Type As (shallow) tympanogram fits best with:
test.explain: Stapes fixation stiffens the system and lowers the peak. Discontinuity gives a very tall Ad peak instead.

test.q: A PTA of 45 dB HL falls into which severity band?
test.explain: In the scheme used here, 41-55 dB HL is moderate hearing loss.

test.q: The chart that plots hearing thresholds across frequencies is called an ___.
test.explain: The audiogram shows thresholds by frequency for each ear.

test.q: Which unit is used to measure pitch on an audiogram?
test.explain: Frequency (pitch) is measured in hertz.

test.q: The middle ear muscle that contracts in the acoustic reflex is the ___.
test.explain: The stapedius contracts in response to loud sound and is supplied by the facial nerve.

kidTest.q: What do you do when you hear a beep in the hearing test?
kidTest.explain: You press a button each time you hear a beep, even a very quiet one.

kidTest.q: What does the soft plug test check?
kidTest.explain: It gently changes the air pressure to see whether the eardrum wiggles.

kidTest.q: What can stop the eardrum from moving well?
kidTest.explain: Gooey fluid behind the eardrum makes it barely move.

kidTest.q: What do the beeps sound like?
kidTest.explain: Some beeps are high like a bird and some are low like a drum.

kidTest.q: The chart of your hearing is called an a _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The audiogram shows the quietest beeps you can hear.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a low-frequency air-bone gap, bone thresholds below 0 dB HL, a normal tympanogram and present acoustic reflexes. What is the most likely cause?
advancedTest.explain: A third-window lesion makes bone conduction supranormal while reflexes stay present. Otosclerosis typically abolishes acoustic reflexes.

advancedTest.q: Why is a 1000 Hz probe tone preferred for tympanometry in young infants?
choices: Infant ears respond best to higher sounds
A 1000 Hz probe measures canal volume more exactly
Infant eardrums are too stiff to move at 226 Hz
Compliant canal walls can mask effusion at 226 Hz
advancedTest.explain: Infant canals are compliant and their ears are mass-influenced, so a 226 Hz probe can show falsely normal peaks despite effusion.

advancedTest.q: Why does the Carhart notch often improve after successful stapes surgery?
choices: Surgery removes cross-hearing to the opposite ear
Steroids given after surgery restore cochlear function
Surgery repairs damaged hair cells near 2 kHz
The notch is a mechanical artifact of stapes fixation
advancedTest.explain: The notch reflects lost middle ear contribution to bone conduction, not true cochlear damage, so it recovers when the stapes moves again.

advancedTest.q: A patient has mild sensorineural loss but absent acoustic reflexes and very poor word recognition in one ear. What is the best next step?
choices: MRI of the internal auditory canals
Fit a hearing aid and reassess later
Repeat the tympanogram in six months
advancedTest.explain: Findings out of proportion to the pure-tone loss suggest retrocochlear disease, such as vestibular schwannoma, which needs MRI.

lessons.title: Bedside Vestibular Exam: Head Impulse, Nystagmus and Dix-Hallpike

levels.kid:
Deep inside each ear is a tiny balance sensor. It is filled with fluid, like a snow globe. When your head moves, the fluid moves, and your brain knows which way you turned.

Your balance sensors are also connected to your eyes. That is why you can read a sign while walking. Your eyes stay steady even when your head bounces!

When someone feels dizzy, doctors look closely at the eyes. They might turn the head quickly to see if the eyes stay locked on the doctor's nose. They watch for **nystagmus**, which means the eyes jiggle back and forth on their own. They might also lay the person down with the head turned, to find loose "crystals" in the ear that cause spinning.
levels.hs:
The **vestibular system** in the inner ear senses head motion. Three **semicircular canals** detect turning, and two organs, the **utricle** and **saccule**, sense gravity and straight-line movement. These sensors drive the **vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)**, which moves your eyes opposite to your head so your vision stays stable.

When a patient has **vertigo** (a false sense of spinning), a bedside exam can show where the problem is:
- **Nystagmus**: involuntary rhythmic eye movement with a slow drift and a fast corrective jerk. It is named by the direction of the fast phase.
- **Head impulse test**: the examiner quickly turns the patient's head while the patient stares at the examiner's nose. If one inner ear is weak, the eyes are dragged along with the head and then make a catch-up jump, called a **corrective saccade**.
- **Dix-Hallpike maneuver**: the patient is moved from sitting to lying with the head turned 45 degrees and tipped slightly back over the edge of the bed.

Real example: a woman gets brief spinning every time she rolls over in bed. During Dix-Hallpike with her right ear down, her eyes beat upward and twist toward the lower ear for about 20 seconds after a short delay. This points to **benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)**: loose calcium carbonate crystals (**otoconia**) have drifted into the right posterior canal.
levels.college:
The bedside vestibular exam tests the VOR and checks the central pathways that control it. Abnormal eye movements are the main sign.

**Nystagmus basics**
- **Peripheral** (labyrinth or vestibular nerve): unidirectional and horizontal-torsional. It beats away from the weak side. Looking toward the fast phase makes it stronger (**Alexander's law**), and fixating on a target suppresses it. Frenzel goggles block fixation, so they help reveal it.
- **Central** (brainstem or cerebellum): may be purely vertical (downbeat or upbeat), purely torsional, or **direction-changing** with gaze. Fixation does not suppress it.

**Head impulse test (HIT)**: the examiner makes small (about 10-20 degree), fast, unpredictable rotations of the head in the plane of the horizontal canal. A healthy VOR keeps the eyes on target. With a unilateral peripheral loss, a turn *toward* the affected side produces a **catch-up saccade**. Vestibular neuritis gives an abnormal HIT. A normal HIT in a patient with constant vertigo and nystagmus is worrying for stroke.

**Test of skew**: alternate cover testing reveals a vertical misalignment of the eyes (**skew deviation**). This suggests a brainstem lesion.

**Dix-Hallpike** detects posterior-canal BPPV, the most common form. A positive test shows:
- Latency of a few seconds
- Upbeating torsional nystagmus, with the top pole of the eye beating toward the lower ear
- Crescendo-decrescendo course lasting under a minute
- Fatigue with repeated testing

The **supine roll test** evaluates horizontal-canal BPPV. Treatment of posterior-canal BPPV is the **Epley** canalith repositioning maneuver.
levels.phd:
The HIT follows from Ewald's laws. In the horizontal canal, ampullopetal endolymph flow is excitatory. Excitation can drive primary vestibular afferents from a resting rate near 90 spikes/s up to several hundred spikes/s. Inhibition can only silence them, which is a floor of zero. A high-acceleration rotation toward a lesioned side therefore relies on inhibition of the intact contralateral canal, and this saturates. The result is a VOR gain deficit. Normal gain is close to 1.0. Halmagyi and Curthoys described the clinical HIT in 1988.

**Video HIT (vHIT)** quantifies gain and separates **overt** saccades from **covert** saccades. Overt saccades occur after the head stops and are visible at the bedside. Covert saccades occur during the head movement and are invisible to the naked eye. This explains false-negative bedside HITs. vHIT can test all six canals, including the LARP and RALP vertical pairs.

**HINTS** (Kattah et al., Stroke 2009) combines Head Impulse, Nystagmus type and Test of Skew. It is applied in the acute vestibular syndrome: continuous vertigo for over 24 hours, with nystagmus, nausea and unsteady gait. A "dangerous" finding is any of the following:
- A normal HIT
- Direction-changing nystagmus
- Skew deviation

HINTS was about 100% sensitive for stroke in that cohort. Early diffusion-weighted MRI was falsely negative in roughly 12% of strokes within 48 hours. Adding bedside hearing testing ("HINTS plus") catches AICA infarcts. Labyrinthine artery ischemia can mimic neuritis with an abnormal HIT, and new hearing loss is the clue.

The Dix-Hallpike pattern is explained by canalithiasis. Otoconia sink through the posterior canal and deflect the cupula ampullofugally. This is excitatory for vertical canals. The response follows the canal's excitatory connections to the ipsilateral superior oblique and contralateral inferior rectus. Latency reflects the time otoconia take to move, and fatigability reflects their dispersal.

In horizontal-canal BPPV, geotropic nystagmus means canalithiasis. Apogeotropic nystagmus suggests otoconia stuck near or on the cupula (cupulolithiasis).
levels.expert:
HINTS performs well only in the right patient. It is validated for the continuous acute vestibular syndrome *with* spontaneous nystagmus. Applied to episodic or positional dizziness, or to patients without nystagmus, an abnormal HIT is uninterpretable. Studies of emergency physicians show lower accuracy than in neuro-otology hands. Guidelines such as the 2023 SAEM GRACE-3 recommend HINTS only for trained examiners. The **TiTrATE** approach (timing, triggers, targeted exam) reframes triage around timing and triggers rather than the vague word "dizzy." Its categories are:
- Acute vestibular syndrome: use HINTS
- Spontaneous episodic vestibular syndrome: consider vestibular migraine, TIA or Ménière disease
- Triggered episodic vestibular syndrome: use Dix-Hallpike and roll tests

Pitfalls:
- **Truncal ataxia**: inability to sit or stand unaided favors a cerebellar stroke even when other signs look peripheral.
- **Cervical spine**: in rheumatoid disease or neck injury, the Dix-Hallpike can be replaced by the **side-lying test**.
- **Mimics**: persistent positional nystagmus without latency or fatigue, pure downbeat nystagmus on positioning, or failure to respond to repositioning suggests central positional nystagmus. Examples are a fourth-ventricle tumour, Chiari malformation or cerebellar lesions, which require MRI.
- **Bilateral vestibulopathy**: aminoglycoside (gentamicin) ototoxicity gives bilaterally abnormal HITs. It may show no nystagmus but causes oscillopsia while walking. A **dynamic visual acuity** test exposes it.
- **Drugs**: vestibular suppressants and alcohol blunt nystagmus. Phenytoin and lithium can produce gaze-evoked or downbeat nystagmus.

Recent advances include smartphone and goggle-based video-oculography and AI analysis of nystagmus recorded at triage. Their aim is to deliver expert-level HINTS where specialists are scarce. **SHIMP** (suppression head impulse) paradigms complement vHIT when residual vestibular function is low.

Open questions remain. One is whether device-based HINTS can reduce both missed posterior circulation strokes and the use of CT, which has poor sensitivity for posterior fossa infarction. Another is how to handle the substantial group of acute vestibular syndrome patients with mixed signs.

keyPoints: The VOR keeps the eyes stable; bedside tests probe it
Nystagmus is named by its fast phase; peripheral nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation
Abnormal head impulse with catch-up saccade means peripheral loss on the side turned toward
HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) screens for stroke in acute vestibular syndrome
Dix-Hallpike: latent, upbeat-torsional, fatiguing nystagmus diagnoses posterior-canal BPPV
Epley maneuver repositions otoconia in posterior-canal BPPV

test.q: By convention, the direction of nystagmus is named after its:
test.explain: Nystagmus is named for the fast phase, even though the slow drift is the abnormal component.

test.q: During a head impulse test, a catch-up saccade after turning the head to the left suggests:
test.explain: The catch-up saccade appears when the head is turned toward the weak side, here the left.

test.q: Which nystagmus feature most suggests a central (brainstem or cerebellar) cause?
test.explain: Direction-changing nystagmus is a central sign; the other features fit peripheral nystagmus.

test.q: What do the letters of HINTS stand for?
choices: Head tilt, Inner ear, Neck, Tympanum, Saccule
Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew
test.explain: HINTS combines the head impulse test, nystagmus type and test of skew.

test.q: A positive Dix-Hallpike for posterior-canal BPPV typically shows nystagmus that is:
choices: Purely horizontal and unchanged on repeat testing
Delayed, upbeat-torsional and fading within a minute
Immediate, downbeating and lasting for many minutes
Absent in the eyes but felt as neck stiffness
test.explain: Latency, upbeat-torsional direction, a brief crescendo-decrescendo course and fatigue are classic for posterior-canal BPPV.

test.q: What causes BPPV?
choices: Excess endolymph pressure in the cochlea
Loose otoconia moving in a semicircular canal
A small infarct in the cerebellum
test.explain: Displaced calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) drift into a canal and abnormally deflect the cupula.

test.q: In a patient with constant vertigo and nystagmus, a normal head impulse test is worrying because it suggests:
choices: Bilateral wax in the ear canals
test.explain: In the acute vestibular syndrome, a normal HIT means the peripheral VOR is intact, so the cause may be central, such as a brainstem or cerebellar stroke. Vestibular neuritis would give an abnormal HIT.

test.q: Alternate cover testing that reveals a vertical eye misalignment is detecting:
test.explain: Skew deviation is the vertical misalignment found by the test of skew, and it points to a brainstem lesion.

test.q: Which test is used to evaluate horizontal-canal BPPV?
test.explain: The supine roll test assesses the horizontal canal. Dix-Hallpike targets the posterior canal, and Epley is a treatment.

test.q: What is the reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head motion to keep vision steady? (abbreviation or full name)
test.explain: The vestibulo-ocular reflex keeps the image stable on the retina during head movement.

test.q: The ___ maneuver is the canalith repositioning treatment for posterior-canal BPPV.
test.explain: The Epley maneuver guides the otoconia out of the posterior canal and back into the utricle.

test.q: Peripheral nystagmus grows stronger when looking toward the fast phase, a rule called ___'s law.
test.explain: Alexander's law describes this gaze-dependent increase in peripheral nystagmus.

kidTest.q: Where are your balance sensors?
kidTest.explain: The balance sensors sit deep inside the inner ear.

kidTest.q: What fills the balance sensors?
kidTest.explain: They are filled with fluid that moves when your head moves, like a snow globe.

kidTest.q: What does a doctor look at to check balance?
kidTest.explain: The balance system is linked to the eyes, so eye movements show how it is working.

kidTest.q: What can loose crystals in the ear cause?
kidTest.explain: Crystals in the wrong place make the brain think the head is spinning.

kidTest.q: When eyes jiggle back and forth on their own, it is called n _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Nystagmus means eyes moving back and forth by themselves.

advancedTest.q: Why does a head impulse toward a lesioned horizontal canal reveal the deficit even though the opposite canal is intact?
choices: The intact canal relies on inhibition, which saturates near zero firing
The lesioned canal fires faster and overrides the intact canal
Otoconia from the lesioned canal block flow in the intact canal
Rapid rotation directly stimulates the extraocular muscles instead
advancedTest.explain: By Ewald's second law, inhibition can only silence afferents, so the intact contralateral canal cannot fully encode a fast rotation away from itself.

advancedTest.q: A bedside HIT looks normal but vHIT shows low gain with saccades. The best explanation is:
choices: Covert saccades hidden during the movement
advancedTest.explain: Covert saccades occur during the head turn, so they are invisible to the eye but detected by video recording.

advancedTest.q: Acute vestibular syndrome, abnormal HIT, unidirectional nystagmus, no skew, but new unilateral hearing loss. The key concern is:
advancedTest.explain: HINTS plus adds hearing. Labyrinthine ischemia from the AICA territory can mimic neuritis with an abnormal HIT, and new hearing loss is the clue.

advancedTest.q: Positional downbeat nystagmus with no latency that persists and does not fatigue most strongly suggests:
advancedTest.explain: A lack of latency and fatigue, a pure downbeat pattern and persistence are central features. Possible causes include a fourth-ventricle or cerebellar lesion, so MRI is needed.

lessons.title: Anterior Rhinoscopy and Flexible Nasolaryngoscopy

levels.kid:
Doctors who look after ears, noses and throats have special tools to peek inside your head without any cutting.

First, they look up your nose. They gently open your nostril with a little tool that spreads it, like holding a curtain open. A bright light shows the wall in the middle of your nose and the soft bumps on the sides.

To see deeper, they use a thin, bendy camera, about as wide as a spaghetti noodle. It slides through your nose and curves down to look at your voice box. That is the part that makes your voice. The doctor can ask you to say "eeee" and watch two tiny folds wiggle together.

It can tickle, but you stay awake and can talk the whole time.
levels.hs:
Two common ways to look inside the nose and throat are **anterior rhinoscopy** and **flexible nasolaryngoscopy**.

**Anterior rhinoscopy** means looking into the front of the nose. The doctor uses a **nasal speculum**, a small hinged tool that gently widens the nostril, plus a headlight. They can see:
- The **nasal septum**, the wall dividing left and right sides. It may be bent (a **deviated septum**).
- The **inferior turbinates**, curled bony shelves covered in soft tissue that warm and moisten air. They swell with allergies.
- Bleeding points, crusts, or growths such as **nasal polyps**.

This view only reaches the front part of the nose. To see further back, doctors use a **flexible nasolaryngoscope**: a thin, steerable fiberoptic or camera-tipped tube passed through the nose while the patient sits up and stays awake. It shows the back of the nose (**nasopharynx**), the base of the tongue, and the **larynx** (voice box), including the **vocal folds**.

Example: a teacher has had a hoarse voice for six weeks. Using the scope, the ENT doctor watches her vocal folds move as she says "eee" and finds small swellings called **vocal fold nodules**, caused by voice strain. The usual treatment is voice therapy rather than surgery.

Before the scope goes in, the nose is usually sprayed with a decongestant and a numbing spray to make it more comfortable.
levels.college:
**Anterior rhinoscopy** is the bedside examination of the anterior nasal cavity using a light source (headlight or head mirror) and a **Thudichum or Killian nasal speculum**. In children, an otoscope with a large speculum is often enough. Lifting the nasal tip helps the view.

Key structures and findings:
- **Septum**: deviation, spurs, perforation, and the anteroinferior **Little's area** (**Kiesselbach's plexus**), the source of most nosebleeds (epistaxis).
- **Inferior turbinate**: pink and moist normally; pale, bluish and boggy in allergic rhinitis; red and swollen in infection or rhinitis medicamentosa.
- **Polyps**: grey, glistening, insensate, mobile; usually bilateral and arising from the middle meatus. A unilateral mass raises concern for inverted papilloma or malignancy.
- **Discharge**: clear, purulent or bloody; unilateral foul discharge in a child suggests a foreign body.
- **Cottle maneuver**: pulling the cheek laterally to test whether the nasal valve is causing obstruction.

Topical decongestion (e.g., oxymetazoline) shrinks the turbinates. This improves the view and separates reversible mucosal swelling from fixed structural blockage.

**Flexible nasolaryngoscopy** (fiberoptic or distal-chip video endoscope) is done in clinic with topical decongestant and anesthetic. The scope passes along the nasal floor or between the middle and inferior turbinates to the nasopharynx. It is then flexed downward to view the oropharynx, hypopharynx and larynx.

Systematic laryngeal assessment:
- Base of tongue, vallecula, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, piriform sinuses, postcricoid region.
- **Vocal fold mobility** on phonation ("eee") and sniffing. Immobility suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.
- Lesions: nodules, polyps, cysts, leukoplakia, tumors.
- Pooling of secretions, suggesting dysphagia.

The main advantage over **indirect mirror laryngoscopy** is that the patient does not need to open wide. That allows natural speech, better tolerance in patients with a strong gag, and video recording.
levels.phd:
Both examinations convert anatomy into function. In the nose, the key physiological variables are airflow resistance and mucosal state. Most nasal resistance is generated at the **internal nasal valve**, bounded by the septum, the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage and the head of the inferior turbinate, with an angle normally around 10–15°. Because flow through a tube scales roughly with the fourth power of radius (Poiseuille), small reductions in valve cross-section cause disproportionate obstruction. This explains why the Cottle and modified Cottle maneuvers, and examination before and after decongestion, are so informative. The **nasal cycle**, alternating congestion of the turbinate venous sinusoids as sympathetic tone falls on one side, means unilateral turbinate swelling on a single exam may be physiological.

Anterior rhinoscopy shows only about the front third of the cavity. The middle meatus, which drains the maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses via the **ostiomeatal complex**, and the sphenoethmoidal recess are generally not visible. Rigid nasal endoscopy (0° and 30°) is therefore needed for staging chronic rhinosinusitis (e.g., the Lund-Kennedy endoscopic score).

In the larynx, flexible endoscopy assesses **neuromuscular function**. Abduction depends on the **posterior cricoarytenoid**, the only abductor, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN). Adduction depends on the lateral cricoarytenoid, interarytenoid and thyroarytenoid. The cricothyroid, innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, tenses the folds for pitch. Unilateral RLN palsy produces a fold in the paramedian position, breathy voice and aspiration risk. Bilateral palsy can leave a narrow glottis with stridor. Separating true paralysis from **cricoarytenoid joint fixation** cannot be done reliably by endoscopy alone; laryngeal EMG or palpation under anesthesia helps.

Standard white light shows fold motion but not the mucosal wave, because folds vibrate at roughly 100–250 Hz, faster than the eye can resolve. **Videostroboscopy** samples successive cycles at slightly offset phases to create an apparent slow-motion wave. Loss of the wave suggests infiltration or scarring (e.g., early glottic carcinoma, sulcus vocalis). High-speed videoendoscopy captures true cycle-by-cycle behavior, including aperiodic vibration that stroboscopy misrepresents.
levels.expert:
In practice, the flexible scope has become an extension of the physical exam. **Distal-chip video endoscopes** have largely replaced fiberoptic bundles, with better resolution and recording. Single-use scopes are increasingly used to avoid reprocessing costs and the risk of cross-infection. Reusable scopes need high-level disinfection, and the COVID-19 era reclassified nasendoscopy as aerosol-generating, prompting PPE protocols that remain in some units.

High-yield applications and pitfalls:
- **Unilateral nasal obstruction with bleeding or unilateral effusion in an adult** requires nasopharyngeal inspection to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma, especially in patients from southern China or with EBV risk. The fossa of Rosenmüller is a classic hiding place.
- **Head and neck cancer workup**: describe subsites, fold mobility and extension (e.g., into the piriform sinus). Fixed hemilarynx upstages glottic cancer to T3. **Narrow-band imaging** highlights abnormal intrapapillary capillary loops, improving detection of dysplasia and early carcinoma.
- **Airway emergencies**: in suspected supraglottitis, deep neck abscess or angioedema, a careful scope in the upright patient guides airway planning. It should be done where a secured airway is immediately available. Pediatric epiglottitis is the exception: avoid instrumentation and examine in theatre.
- **Postoperative voice change** after thyroid or cardiothoracic surgery: document pre- and postoperative fold mobility. The left RLN loops under the aortic arch, so left palsy also points to mediastinal pathology.
- **FEES** (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing) uses the same scope with dyed food boluses to assess penetration, aspiration and residue at the bedside. It complements videofluoroscopy.
- **DISE** (drug-induced sleep endoscopy) examines collapse patterns in obstructive sleep apnea using the VOTE classification. It is used in selecting patients for hypoglossal nerve stimulation.

Common errors: incomplete views of the postcricoid and piriform sinuses, where hypopharyngeal tumors hide; mistaking normal arytenoid asymmetry for paresis; and interpreting a single anterior rhinoscopy without decongestion. Open questions include the role of AI-assisted lesion detection in endoscopic video and the cost-effectiveness of routine stroboscopy for hoarseness. Hoarseness guidelines recommend laryngoscopy when it persists beyond about four weeks or sooner if serious disease is suspected.

keyPoints: Anterior rhinoscopy uses a nasal speculum and light to view the front of the nose
Look at the septum, inferior turbinates, Little's area, polyps and discharge
Decongestion separates mucosal swelling from fixed structural obstruction
Flexible nasolaryngoscopy views nasopharynx, pharynx and larynx in an awake patient
Vocal fold immobility suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
Videostroboscopy reveals the mucosal wave that ordinary light cannot show

test.q: Which instrument gently widens the nostril during anterior rhinoscopy?
test.explain: A nasal speculum, such as a Thudichum, opens the nostril. An otoscope may be used in children, but the standard tool is the speculum.

test.q: Most nosebleeds arise from which area?
test.explain: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the anteroinferior septum is the usual source of epistaxis.

test.q: Pale, bluish, boggy inferior turbinates most suggest:
test.explain: Pale, boggy mucosa is classic for allergic rhinitis. Infection tends to make the mucosa red.

test.q: Why is a decongestant sprayed before examining the nose?
choices: To stop the patient from sneezing
To shrink turbinates and improve the view
To kill bacteria on the mucosa
To dry out any watery discharge
test.explain: Decongestion shrinks the turbinates, giving a better view and separating reversible swelling from fixed blockage.

test.q: A unilateral foul nasal discharge in a young child most suggests:
test.explain: One-sided foul discharge in a child is a classic sign of a foreign body.

test.q: What does flexible nasolaryngoscopy allow that anterior rhinoscopy does not?
choices: A view of the nostril skin
test.explain: The flexible scope reaches the nasopharynx and larynx, so it can show the vocal folds. Anterior rhinoscopy sees only the front of the nose.

test.q: A vocal fold that does not move on phonation suggests a problem with which nerve?
test.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles, so its palsy causes fold immobility.

test.q: Grey, glistening, insensate, mobile masses from the middle meatus are typically:
test.explain: These are the features of nasal polyps, usually bilateral. A unilateral mass raises concern for papilloma or malignancy.

test.q: A key advantage of flexible scopes over mirror laryngoscopy is that the patient can:
test.explain: The flexible scope lets the patient speak naturally without opening wide, and it is better tolerated by people with a strong gag.

test.q: The wall dividing the left and right nasal cavities is the nasal ___.
test.explain: The septum can be deviated, perforated, or bleed from Little's area.

test.q: What maneuver pulls the cheek outward to test whether the nasal valve is causing obstruction?
test.explain: The Cottle maneuver opens the nasal valve. If breathing improves, the valve is contributing to obstruction.

test.q: Small swellings on the vocal folds caused by voice strain are called vocal fold ___.
test.explain: Nodules come from voice overuse and are usually treated with voice therapy.

kidTest.q: What does the doctor use to gently open your nostril?
kidTest.explain: A little tool called a speculum gently spreads the nostril.

kidTest.q: How wide is the bendy camera?
choices: About as wide as a pencil case
About as wide as a noodle
About as wide as a straw cup
kidTest.explain: It is very thin, about as wide as a spaghetti noodle.

kidTest.q: What part does the bendy camera look at deep inside?
kidTest.explain: It curves down to look at the voice box, which makes your voice.

kidTest.q: During the camera test, you are:
kidTest.explain: You stay awake and can even say "eeee."

kidTest.q: The bendy camera goes in through your n _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: It slides through the nose and down to the voice box.

advancedTest.q: Why does a small narrowing at the internal nasal valve cause disproportionate obstruction?
choices: The septum collapses inward whenever pressure falls
Turbinate blood flow rises in step with any narrowing
Mucus production doubles as the airway narrows
Flow scales roughly with radius to the fourth power
advancedTest.explain: By Poiseuille-type relationships, flow depends roughly on radius to the fourth power, so small radius changes have large effects.

advancedTest.q: One exam shows a swollen left inferior turbinate but no symptoms. The best interpretation is:
choices: Possible nasal cycle effect; reassess after decongestion
Likely left inverted papilloma needing biopsy
Probable early nasal polyp on the left
advancedTest.explain: The nasal cycle causes alternating physiological congestion, so one-sided swelling on a single exam can be normal.

advancedTest.q: Stroboscopy shows normal fold motion but an absent mucosal wave on one fold. This most suggests:
choices: Normal vibration at a high pitch
advancedTest.explain: Preserved motion rules against nerve palsy. Loss of the wave points to stiffness from scarring or early carcinoma.

advancedTest.q: A new left vocal fold palsy with no neck surgery should prompt evaluation of the:
advancedTest.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch, so mediastinal disease can cause left palsy.
